Newly hatched individuals of Bathypolypus arcticus emerge from their egg capsules at an age of 400 days [ab = 400 days] when incubated at a stable temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C], a developmental interval that is exceptionally prolonged relative to many shallow-water octopus species. At the moment of hatching, these paralarvae possess a wet weight of 0.250 grams [Wwb = 0.250 grams], a diminutive mass that reflects the substantial yolk investment required to sustain such an extended embryonic period under cold, deep-sea conditions. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after emergence, though the precise timing of first prey capture remains poorly documented for this species. Field observations indicate that the hatchlings are well-developed and capable of benthic locomotion almost immediately, a trait that distinguishes them from the planktonic paralarvae of many other octopuses. The combined constraints of low temperature and limited food availability in the North Atlantic deep sea likely contribute to the slow developmental pace observed in this species, with the lengthy incubation period representing a trade-off between offspring size at hatching and the energetic demands of brooding females.

As the juvenile grows, it undergoes a gradual but steady increase in body mass before reaching the onset of gonadal development. Reproductive maturity in Bathypolypus arcticus is attained when an individual achieves a wet weight of approximately 30 grams [Wwp = approximately 30 grams], a size that typically corresponds to the initiation of gametogenesis and the development of functional reproductive organs. This threshold represents a critical life-history transition, separating the somatic growth phase from the period of reproductive investment. Comparative data from other deep-sea octopus species suggest that the mass at puberty is relatively low in proportion to the maximum adult size, indicating that females may begin allocating resources to reproduction while still actively growing. The attainment of this weight is influenced by local environmental conditions, particularly temperature and food supply, which can accelerate or delay the maturation process. Once this size is reached, individuals are physiologically capable of mating, although successful reproduction also depends on the availability of suitable mates and the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves to support egg production and subsequent brooding.

Females of Bathypolypus arcticus that have completed their reproductive lives typically expire at a wet weight of around 300 grams [Wwi = around 300 grams], which represents the maximum body mass recorded for this species in the wild. This substantial size reflects the considerable somatic growth that occurs between puberty and senescence, during which the octopus may more than decuple its body weight through active foraging on crustacean prey. The wet weight at death is a useful metric for estimating the energetic scope of the species, as it integrates the cumulative effects of food intake, metabolic expenditure, and reproductive output over the entire lifespan. Moribund individuals often exhibit signs of physiological deterioration, including reduced feeding activity and progressive loss of body condition, consistent with a semelparous reproductive strategy common among coleoid cephalopods. The observed maximum mass of 300 grams [Wwi = 300 grams] places Bathypolypus arcticus among the smaller-bodied members of the Octopodidae, a characteristic that is likely linked to the limited productivity of its cold-water habitat and the energetic constraints of a slow life history.

Fecundity in Bathypolypus arcticus has been estimated at 44 eggs per female  when maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], with this value corresponding to a maternal wet weight of approximately 45 grams. This relatively low clutch size, compared to many octopus species that produce thousands of eggs, is consistent with the production of large, yolky eggs that yield well-developed hatchlings capable of direct benthic development. Wood (2000) suggested that females reach maturity around 6 years of age, after which they invest roughly one additional year in brooding the single clutch before dying, a pattern that aligns with the extreme iteroparity observed in some deep-sea octopuses. The low fecundity is compensated by a high per-offspring investment, as each egg must contain sufficient nutrients to sustain the embryo through its 400-day incubation period (400 days) [ab = 400 days] at cold temperatures at a temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C]. This reproductive strategy, characterized by few but large offspring, is typical of species inhabiting stable but resource-poor environments where juvenile survival is maximized at the expense of total fecundity.

The maximum lifespan recorded for female Bathypolypus arcticus under natural conditions is approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years], though this estimate rem at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]ains uncertain. Some populations maintained at 4 °C [T = 4 °C] may exhibit a shorter lifespan of around 3 years [am = 3 years]. Such longevity is remarkable for a cephalopod, most of which complete their life cycles within one to two years, and it positions this species among the longest-lived octopuses known to science. The extended lifespan is thought to be a consequence of the cold, deep-sea environment, which depresses metabolic rates and slows the pace of aging-related physiological processes. Females likely spend several years as juveniles slowly accumulating biomass before reaching the pubertal weight of 30 grams [Wwp = 30 grams], after which they may reproduce only once before succumbing to post-reproductive senescence. The age at hatching of 400 days [ab = 400 days] at 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C] further underscores the slow tempo of life in this species, with the entire pre-reproductive period spanning many years. Future studies employing statolith-based age estimation and mark-recapture techniques will be essential to refine our understanding of longevity and population dynamics in this enigmatic deep-sea octopus.
